title: Kepler's Laws
subtitle: Measure the shape, pacing and timing of real orbits
body:
Step 1 of 26 read

Three questions about an orbit

What path does a planet follow around its star, and what sets how fast it moves and how long its year is? You will answer it in the live orbit view: predict first, then measure distances, speeds and years in orbits you choose.

Johannes Kepler answered it four hundred years ago from positions of Mars measured without a telescope. Why he trusted them comes after your first prediction.

💡 While an investigation is running, clicking selects an object without opening the inspector card, and placing new objects is switched off so a stray click cannot alter the system you are measuring.

body:

Where is the star?

An ellipse has a center, halfway along its long diameter, and two special points called foci, one on each side of the center.

Look at the orange body's path and where the star sits inside it. Commit to an answer before measuring anything: the next step gives you a way to check it.

title: Kepler's Laws
subtitle: Measure the shape, pacing and timing of real orbits
body:
Step 26 of 26 read

Where this leaves you

The three laws are not three separate facts. One pull toward the star, weakening as the square of the distance, produces all of them, which is why they hold for TRAPPIST-1 as they do here. They describe a light body going round a much heavier one: when the two masses are close, as in a pair of stars, both move, and the period depends on their sum.
